fathers/john-chrysostom/summary: Antiochene preacher (c. 349–407), trained in rhetoric and in Diodore’s literal exegesis, whose sermons on Scripture, wealth and the poor earned him the name ‘Golden Mouth’; as archbishop of Constantinople he clashed with the court and died in exile.
fathers/john-chrysostom/story:
John was born in Antioch around 349, the son of an army officer who died young; his mother Anthusa raised him and refused to remarry. Church historians report that he studied rhetoric under the great pagan sophist Libanius, who allegedly would have named John his successor ‘had not the Christians stolen him’. Baptised around 368 by Bishop Meletius, he joined the asketerion of Diodore (later bishop of Tarsus), where with Theodore of Mopsuestia he learned the Antiochene method of historical, grammatical exegesis.

Around 372 he withdrew to the mountains near Antioch, living under an old Syrian monk and then alone in a cave, until severe ascetic practices ruined his health. Returning to the city, he was ordained deacon in 381 and priest in 386, and for twelve years was Antioch’s principal preacher. His homilies on Genesis, Matthew, John and Paul’s letters, delivered in series, are the largest body of patristic preaching to survive. In 387, when rioters toppled the statues of Theodosius and the city feared reprisals, his Homilies on the Statues comforted and admonished the population. His eight sermons Against the Judaizers (386–387), aimed at Christians who attended synagogue festivals, use violent invective that later fed Christian anti-Judaism.

In 397 he was virtually kidnapped and brought to Constantinople to become archbishop, consecrated in February 398 by a reluctant Theophilus of Alexandria. He cut episcopal expenses, founded hospitals, disciplined clergy and monks, and preached against the luxury of the rich, alienating powerful figures including the Empress Eudoxia. When he received the ‘Tall Brothers’, Origenist monks expelled by Theophilus, his enemies combined: the Synod of the Oak (403), near Chalcedon, deposed him. Recalled after popular uproar, he was exiled again in 404 to Cucusus in Armenia, from where his letters to the deaconess Olympias and to supporters such as Pope Innocent I continued. Ordered further away to Pityus on the Black Sea, he died on the road at Comana in Pontus on 14 September 407, saying ‘Glory to God for all things’.

In 438 his relics were brought back to Constantinople and the emperor Theodosius II publicly begged forgiveness for his parents. From the sixth century he was called Chrysostomos, ‘golden-mouthed’. The principal Eucharistic liturgy of the Byzantine rite bears his name; its anaphora is probably connected with him, though the rite as celebrated today developed over centuries.

Chrysostom’s exegesis is pastoral and moral rather than speculative: he reads Paul as a model of love and labour, insists that the Eucharist demands care for the poor, and treats the household as a ‘little church’. Modern readers praise his social preaching and criticise his anti-Jewish sermons; both belong to his legacy.
fathers/john-chrysostom/roots/0/text: Trained in the Second Sophistic tradition (reportedly by Libanius), he mastered vivid diatribe, ekphrasis and audience address, adapted for Christian homily.
fathers/john-chrysostom/roots/1/text: Diodore of Tarsus taught him Antiochene exegesis attentive to history (historia) and the author’s intention, sparing in allegory.
fathers/john-chrysostom/roots/2/text: He preached whole series on Genesis and the Psalms and saw Old Testament saints as moral examples, while reading the Old Testament through the economy of salvation in Christ.
fathers/john-chrysostom/roots/3/text: His years in the Syrian mountains shaped his ideal of Christian life; he urged lay people in the city to live with monastic simplicity.
fathers/john-chrysostom/roots/4/text: Popular Stoic and Cynic moral themes — contempt for wealth, self-mastery, ‘no one is harmed except by himself’ — recur in his sermons in Christian form.
fathers/john-chrysostom/roots/5/text: As bishop of the imperial capital he was caught between court, aristocracy, rival patriarchs and monks, and fell victim to ecclesiastical politics.
fathers/john-chrysostom/keyTeachings/0: Care for the poor as inseparable from worship: Christ is honoured in the needy
fathers/john-chrysostom/keyTeachings/1: The priesthood as a burden of great responsibility (On the Priesthood)
fathers/john-chrysostom/keyTeachings/2: Literal, historical exegesis with moral application; Paul as the model Christian
fathers/john-chrysostom/keyTeachings/3: The household as a ‘little church’ and the dignity of Christian marriage
fathers/john-chrysostom/keyTeachings/4: Divine ‘condescension’ (synkatabasis): God adapts revelation to human weakness
fathers/john-chrysostom/keyTeachings/5: Real presence and awe before the Eucharistic sacrifice
fathers/john-chrysostom/works/0/note: Six books in dialogue form on the dignity and dangers of the priestly office.
fathers/john-chrysostom/works/1/note: Ninety homilies on Matthew and eighty-eight on John, preached at Antioch.
fathers/john-chrysostom/works/2/note: Thirty-two homilies; a classic of Pauline exegesis much used by the Reformers.
fathers/john-chrysostom/works/3/note: Forty-four homilies with extensive moral and social teaching.
fathers/john-chrysostom/works/4/note: Twenty-one sermons preached during the crisis following the Antioch riot.
fathers/john-chrysostom/works/5/note: Eight sermons attacking Christian participation in Jewish festivals; a key text in the history of Christian anti-Judaism.
fathers/john-chrysostom/works/6/title: Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom
fathers/john-chrysostom/works/6/note: The usual Eucharistic liturgy of the Byzantine rite, attributed to him.
fathers/john-chrysostom/doctrineContribu: The most widely read representative of Antiochene exegesis, combining historical reading with pastoral application.
His preaching on wealth, almsgiving and slavery made him a central patristic voice for Christian social teaching.
On the Priesthood and his Eucharistic homilies shaped Eastern and Western understandings of ministry and sacrifice.
The Byzantine Divine Liturgy bears his name and is celebrated daily throughout the Orthodox and Byzantine Catholic world.
His homilies on Ephesians 5 present marriage as an icon of Christ and the Church and the household as a church in miniature.
fathers/john-chrysostom/laterInfluence/0: With Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus one of the Three Holy Hierarchs (30 January); the model of the Orthodox preacher and pastor.
fathers/john-chrysostom/laterInfluence/1: Calvin admired his plain exegesis while disagreeing with him on free will; Cranmer’s Book of Common Prayer included a ‘Prayer of St Chrysostom’.
fathers/john-chrysostom/laterInfluence/2: His sermons on the poor are frequently cited in modern papal teaching on wealth and the universal destination of goods.
fathers/john-chrysostom/laterInfluence/3: His Adversus Judaeos was later exploited by anti-Jewish polemicists, and since the Holocaust has been a focus of Christian self-examination.
fathers/john-chrysostom/reception/0/text: One of the Three Holy Hierarchs and universal teachers; feasts 13 November, 27 January (translation of relics) and 30 January.
fathers/john-chrysostom/reception/1/text: Declared Doctor of the Church (1568); patron of preachers; feast 13 September.
fathers/john-chrysostom/reception/2/text: Venerated in the Coptic, Syriac and Armenian churches; many of his homilies were translated into Syriac, Armenian and Coptic.
fathers/john-chrysostom/reception/3/text: Valued for exegesis and preaching; Anglicans commemorate him on 13 September.
fathers/john-chrysostom/reception/4/text: His anti-Jewish sermons are widely acknowledged as harmful and are critically studied (e.g. Robert Wilken, John Chrysostom and the Jews, 1983).
fathers/john-chrysostom/controversies/0: The anti-Jewish sermons (Adversus Judaeos) and their later use
fathers/john-chrysostom/controversies/1: His deposition at the Synod of the Oak (403) and exile, driven by Theophilus of Alexandria and the court
fathers/john-chrysostom/controversies/2: The Origenist controversy and his reception of the Tall Brothers
fathers/john-chrysostom/controversies/3: Authorship and development of the liturgy bearing his name
fathers/john-chrysostom/quote/text: Do you wish to honour the body of Christ? Do not despise him when he is naked. Do not honour him here in the church with silken garments while you neglect him outside where he is cold and naked.
fathers/theodore-of-mopsuestia/summary: Antiochene bishop and biblical scholar (c. 350–428), the leading exponent of historical exegesis and of a ‘two-nature’ Christology; honoured as ‘the Interpreter’ by the Church of the East but posthumously condemned at Constantinople in 553.
fathers/theodore-of-mopsuestia/story:
Theodore was born in Antioch around 350 into a wealthy family; his brother Polychronius became bishop of Apamea. He studied rhetoric, reportedly under Libanius, together with John Chrysostom, and followed John into the asketerion of Diodore. When he left for a time, apparently intending to marry and pursue a career, Chrysostom’s letters To Theodore after his Fall (traditionally identified as addressed to him) urged him back. He was ordained priest at Antioch around 383 and in 392 became bishop of Mopsuestia in Cilicia, which he governed for thirty-six years. In 394 he preached at a synod in Constantinople before Theodosius I.

Theodore was the most rigorous exegete of the Antiochene school. Against what he saw as Alexandrian allegory, which dissolved history into symbols, he insisted on the historical sense and on the intention of the biblical author. He assigned most psalms to the historical setting of David or later Israel and held that only a handful (Psalms 2, 8, 45 and 110) speak directly of Christ; he read the Song of Songs as Solomon’s love poetry, and reportedly questioned the place of some books in the canon. Typology was allowed only where a real historical correspondence existed. His commentary on the Minor Prophets survives in Greek, that on John in Syriac and those on Paul’s minor letters in Latin.

His theology centres on the two ‘ages’ (katastaseis): this mortal, changeable age, and the immortal, unchangeable age inaugurated by Christ’s resurrection, into which believers enter sacramentally through baptism and the Eucharist. Against Apollinarius, who denied Christ a human mind, he insisted that the Word assumed a complete human being, with a human soul and will that genuinely struggled and grew. He described the union as an indwelling of the Word in the ‘assumed man’ by divine good pleasure (eudokia), forming one prosopon (person or presentation). Critics held that this made Christ two subjects joined by grace.

Theodore died in 428, the year his probable pupil Nestorius became bishop of Constantinople. In the controversy that followed, Cyril of Alexandria and Rabbula of Edessa attacked Theodore as Nestorius’s source, while Antiochene loyalists defended him. In the sixth century Justinian, seeking reconciliation with the miaphysites, had his person and writings condemned as one of the ‘Three Chapters’ at the Second Council of Constantinople (553). Much of his Greek work perished as a result.

In the Syriac East, by contrast, his works were translated at the School of Edessa in the early fifth century and became the curriculum of the School of Nisibis; synods of the Church of the East made his exegesis normative. The discovery and publication of his Catechetical Homilies in Syriac by Alphonse Mingana (1932–33) revived interest in him as a theologian of the sacraments and a forerunner of historical-critical exegesis.
fathers/theodore-of-mopsuestia/roots/0/t: Diodore of Tarsus formed him in the Antiochene exegetical method and the anti-Apollinarian, two-nature Christology.
fathers/theodore-of-mopsuestia/roots/1/t: Ancient grammatical and rhetorical study (attention to hypothesis, author’s intention and historia) underlies Antiochene exegesis, as Frances Young has shown.
fathers/theodore-of-mopsuestia/roots/2/t: He read the Old Testament first as the history of Israel and its prophets, limiting direct messianic prophecy to a few texts.
fathers/theodore-of-mopsuestia/roots/3/t: Some scholars detect affinities with Jewish historical interpretation of the Psalms and Prophets, though the extent of direct contact is debated.
fathers/theodore-of-mopsuestia/roots/4/t: His concern for complete natures and his analytical precision about ‘nature’ and ‘person’ reflect the logical training of the schools, sometimes linked to Aristotelian categories.
fathers/theodore-of-mopsuestia/keyTeachi: Historical exegesis: Scripture interpreted according to its literal-historical sense and the author’s intention
Typology only where genuine historical correspondence exists; very few direct messianic prophecies
Christ’s complete humanity, including a human soul and free will, against Apollinarius
The union of the Word with the ‘assumed man’ by good pleasure (eudokia) in one prosopon
The two ages: the present mortal state and the future immortal state anticipated in baptism and Eucharist
Human freedom and moral struggle as essential to salvation
fathers/theodore-of-mopsuestia/works/0/n: The only major commentary surviving complete in Greek.
fathers/theodore-of-mopsuestia/works/1/t: Commentary on the Gospel of John
fathers/theodore-of-mopsuestia/works/1/n: Preserved in Syriac, with Greek fragments.
fathers/theodore-of-mopsuestia/works/2/t: Commentaries on the Minor Pauline Epistles
fathers/theodore-of-mopsuestia/works/2/n: Preserved in a Latin translation under the name of Ambrose.
fathers/theodore-of-mopsuestia/works/3/n: Sixteen homilies on the Creed, the Lord’s Prayer, baptism and the Eucharist, preserved in Syriac and published by Mingana (1932–33).
fathers/theodore-of-mopsuestia/works/4/n: Fifteen books, now fragmentary; central in the later condemnation.
fathers/theodore-of-mopsuestia/works/5/n: An early work, partly preserved, showing his historicising approach.
fathers/theodore-of-mopsuestia/doctrineC: Classic statement of Antiochene ‘Word–man’ Christology, defending Christ’s full humanity; condemned in 553 as dividing Christ, but foundational for the Church of the East.
Most systematic practitioner of Antiochene historical exegesis.
His Catechetical Homilies are a major witness to late fourth-century baptismal and Eucharistic liturgy and theology.
His doctrine of the two ages frames salvation as passage from mortality and mutability to immortality.
fathers/theodore-of-mopsuestia/laterInfl: Revered as ‘the Interpreter’ (Mpaššqānā); his works, translated by Ibas and others at Edessa, formed the curriculum of the School of Nisibis and defined East Syriac theology.
Seen by Cyril and later by Justinian as the source of Nestorius’s errors; his condemnation in 553 (the Three Chapters) divided the West, causing schism in northern Italy.
His Pauline commentaries circulated under Ambrose’s name, and his exegetical method reached the West through Junillus Africanus’s handbook (c. 542).
Since the twentieth century he has been studied as a precursor of historical-critical exegesis and as a theologian of Christ’s genuine humanity.
fathers/theodore-of-mopsuestia/reception: Church of the East (Assyrian and Ancient)
Venerated among the ‘Greek doctors’ with Diodore and Nestorius; his exegesis remains authoritative.
Condemned by the Second Council of Constantinople (553); modern ecumenical dialogue with the Assyrian Church of the East has eased the Christological divide without lifting the condemnation.
Rejected as a forerunner of Nestorius in Syriac Orthodox, Coptic and Armenian tradition.
Valued as a historical exegete and for his emphasis on Christ’s human agency.
fathers/theodore-of-mopsuestia/controver: Whether his Christology truly divided Christ into two subjects, or was a legitimate emphasis on full humanity misread through Nestorius
Posthumous condemnation of a person who died in communion with the Church, debated even in 553
Reliability of the extracts used against him, some of which may have been selectively quoted or altered
His relationship to Pelagian ideas: he hosted Julian of Eclanum and wrote against those who say humans sin ‘by nature’
